question: Did Florida repeal no-fault insurance?
aliases: is PIP still required in Florida
did Florida get rid of personal injury protection
shortAnswer: No. Two attempts have failed and the Florida Motor Vehicle No-Fault Law is still in place. CS/CS/SB 54 in 2021 was titled Motor Vehicle Insurance and its description included repealing the provisions comprising the No-Fault Law; the Senate's bill history records that it was vetoed by the Governor on June 29, 2021 [S:fl-sb-54-2021-bill]. HB 1181 in 2025 would have repealed provisions relating to application of the law and was indefinitely postponed and withdrawn from consideration, dying in committee [S:fl-hb1181-2025-bill].
assumes: You are asking about the statutory requirement rather than about any particular insurer's product.
The question concerns Florida personal auto insurance, which is where the No-Fault Law operates.
The position is as the bill histories record it on the access date; a later session could change it.
why:
This is a question worth answering carefully because the wrong answer is widely repeated, and it is repeated for an understandable reason: a repeal bill passed the legislature.

CS/CS/SB 54 in the 2021 session was titled Motor Vehicle Insurance, and its description includes repealing provisions which comprise the Florida Motor Vehicle No-Fault Law [S:fl-sb-54-2021-bill]. Coverage of a bill passing is easy to find. What followed is less visible: the Senate's own bill history shows an entry dated June 29, 2021 reading that the bill was vetoed by the Governor, with companion bills passed [S:fl-sb-54-2021-bill]. The history also records a veto message received on November 12, 2021 and transmitted to the Secretary of State on March 15, 2022 [S:fl-sb-54-2021-bill].

A second attempt followed. HB 1181 in 2025 was also titled Motor Vehicle Insurance and would have repealed provisions relating to application of the Florida Motor Vehicle No-Fault Law and revised motor vehicle insurance coverage [S:fl-hb1181-2025-bill]. It was indefinitely postponed and withdrawn from consideration on May 3, 2025, and died in the Judiciary Committee on June 16, 2025 [S:fl-hb1181-2025-bill].

So the practical answer is that personal injury protection remains required. Every owner or registrant of a motor vehicle required to be registered and licensed in Florida must maintain the required security [S:fl-stat-627-733], and the PIP benefit is $10,000 in medical and disability benefits with $5,000 in death benefits [S:fl-stat-627-736].

The reason this matters beyond trivia is that people make coverage decisions on it. Someone who believes Florida has moved to a fault-based system may assume their own medical costs will be recovered from the other driver, and may not treat the 14-day condition on PIP medical benefits as urgent [S:fl-stat-627-736].
whatChanges: A future legislative session. Both attempts recorded here failed, but this is a question about the current state of the law rather than a permanent answer [S:fl-sb-54-2021-bill][S:fl-hb1181-2025-bill].
Nothing about any particular policy. The requirement is statutory and applies to the owner or registrant of a vehicle required to be registered in Florida [S:fl-stat-627-733].
Whether you are reading about the bill or about the law, which is the distinction that produces the confusion [S:fl-sb-54-2021-bill].
variability: This records the position as the Florida Senate's own bill histories state it on the access date. Confirm the current law before relying on it for a decision.
Bill histories describe what happened procedurally. They do not describe what a repeal would have done had it taken effect, and this record does not either.
Other states have their own no-fault positions, and several have repealed or never adopted one.
nextActions: Treat PIP as required and act on its conditions, in particular getting initial services and care within 14 days of an accident [S:fl-stat-627-736].
Check any article claiming repeal against the bill history itself, since both bills are traceable and both failed [S:fl-sb-54-2021-bill][S:fl-hb1181-2025-bill].
Confirm your own policy carries the required security, which is a statutory obligation of the owner or registrant [S:fl-stat-627-733].
If a decision turns on this, verify the current session's bills rather than relying on a record with an access date.
author: Aaron Bollinger
